questions.question: Explain why the headgear working drawing needs more than one view, describe how three views are arranged in first-angle projection and what each shows for an A-frame headgear, and explain how scale and dimension values are handled.
questions.expected_answer: A tower with a sloping back-leg and a sheave at the top cannot be fully described by one face, so three orthographic views are used. In first-angle projection the front view sits in the centre, the top view or plan directly below it, and the side view to the right as seen from the left, with features projected between views so heights and widths align. For an A-frame the front view looks at the face containing the back-leg, showing the A shape, the leg's slope and the sheave height; the side view shows the tower's width and the bracing in that face; the plan shows the base, the footprint and the back-leg's foot, where toppling and the 300 millimetre base constraint are checked. Scale is chosen so the views fit the sheet with room for dimensions, for example 1:5 for a 600 millimetre model on A3, and is written in the title block, while all dimensions are written as full-size model values; if the drawing also represents the real headgear, the model-to-real factor is noted and real dimensions are tabulated beside the drawing.

questions.question: State the line conventions used on the headgear drawing and the rules for dimensioning it, including how bracing nodes, the back-leg and member sizes are given.
questions.expected_answer: Thick continuous lines show visible outlines and edges; thin continuous lines are used for dimension lines, extension lines, hatching and leaders; thin dashed lines show hidden detail such as the back-leg foot under the base plate or a shaft behind a member; thin chain lines show centre lines of the shaft, the sheave axis and gear shafts; break lines shorten long members; construction lines are faint or erased. Each dimension appears once on the view where the feature is clearest, with overall dimensions outermost and positions inside them; bracing nodes are given as a chain of dimensions up a leg; the back-leg is dimensioned by the position of its foot on the base and its top on the tower, never by its sloping length, with an angle given only where the builder must set one; member sizes such as 6 millimetre dowel are given as notes with leaders or in the parts list; dimension lines sit outside the outline with small arrowheads, figures above the line in millimetres without units, and extension lines leaving a small gap; joint types are called out with leaders.

questions.question: Describe how the winding mechanism, rope and safety features are shown in the views, what detail views and sections add, and what the parts list contains and what it feeds.
questions.expected_answer: The drum is a rectangle in the front view at the foot of the back-leg or inside the base with its shaft as a chain line and its diameter dimensioned; the motor is a rectangle on its own chain line; the gear train appears in the side view, where shafts are end-on, as pitch circles with tooth counts and centre distances taken from the gear drawing; the rope is a thin line from the drum edge over the sheave and down the shaft centre line to a cage rectangle with the shaft depth dimensioned; the brake pawl or lever is drawn where it acts with its pivot dimensioned, and the bumper and depth pointer are shown and noted. A detail view encloses a small area and redraws it at larger scale, such as the gear plate or the brake pawl, and a section through the tower at a marked cutting plane shows the leg and bracing arrangement and the gear plate fixing. The parts list numbers every member and component with description, material, size, length and quantity, with balloon numbers on the views, and feeds the materials budget and the construction steps; the title block carries title, company, date, scale, projection symbol and a revision letter.
